subject: How to determine a significant WAIC threshold in a GWAS setting?

messages.author: f42b0240615306ac
messages.subject: How to determine a significant WAIC threshold in a GWAS setting?
parts:
Hi Stan,

I just implemented my model with Stan in a genome-wide association study. It worked great. Detailedly, I have 1 million SNP. I run my model for each of them independently. With that, I computed WAIC to quantify the fitness. Now I have 1 million WAIC quantities. I also have a null model, in which no SNP was included. By subtracting the WAIC quantity of the null model, I have the WAIC differences for each of the SNP, which describes how much the model was improved by including each of the SNP.

How to determine a cutoff for the WAIC differences (or original WAIC) to identify the true association? This is reminiscent of multiple comparison correction of p-value in the frequentist framework.

Can I generate a null distribution of the WAIC by shuffling the genotype of each SNP (permutation), from which to compute a p-value for each of the real WAIC?

Also, given that the full posterior distribution of each SNP's effect size was obtained by sampling, can I simply use the 95% CI and not worry about the multiple comparison issue at all?

Xulong

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to determine a significant WAIC threshold in a GWAS setting?
parts:
Hi, if you are comparing just 2 models, you can get a s.e. for Waic as described in this paper:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/loo_stan.pdf
With more than 2 models to compare, it would make sense to fit some sort of hierarchical model to the Waic output; we’ve discussed this idea but have never done it.
A

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: How to determine a significant WAIC threshold in a GWAS setting?
parts: On Monday, November 30, 2015 at 10:23:29 PM UTC+2, Xulong Wang wrote:
> Can I generate a null distribution of the WAIC by shuffling the genotype of each SNP (permutation), from which to compute a p-value for each of the real WAIC?
Yes, you can. This way will get some idea how big difference in WAIC is likely to be significant, but making independent models for each SNP is bad idea.
> Also, given that the full posterior distribution of each SNP's effect size was obtained by sampling, can I simply use the 95% CI and not worry about the multiple comparison issue at all?

If you make independent models, you need to worry about the multiple comparison. 

It would be better to make one hierarchical model for all SNPs. Hierarchcial model with 1 million SNPs is challenging, but here are couple papers
http://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0049445
http://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0029115
and code
http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/bmagwa/
(unfortunately this is not possible yet with Stan)

If the hierarchical model is good, then you don't need to worry about the multiple comparison (see on Andrew's papers).

On Tuesday, December 1, 2015 at 7:17:13 AM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> With more than 2 models to compare, it would make sense to fit some sort of hierarchical model to the Waic output; we’ve discussed this idea but have never done it.

It's better to make hierarchical model for SNPs than for WAIC output. Making a hierarchical model for WAIC output would be as difficult as for SNP data, but less efficient as you need to make first the independent models, and WAIC summary will discard information compared to the original data.

Aki
